lesson_emails.subject: Your Kubernetes journey starts now
topics_covered: What Kubernetes is and the problem it solves
key_concepts: Kubernetes as a container orchestrator
Declarative configuration
Pods as the smallest deployable unit
Clusters as sets of machines working together

lesson_emails.subject: Day 2: Deployments - The Magic of Self-Healing Applications
lesson_emails.file_name: Day 2_ Deployments - The Magic of Self-Healing Applications.eml
key_concepts: Pods are ephemeral and can die at any time
Deployments manage pods and ensure desired replica count
Self-healing: Kubernetes automatically replaces failed pods
ReplicaSets sit between Deployments and Pods
Labels and selectors organize and find objects
what_you_learned_today: Pods are ephemeral and can die at any time. They won't come back on their own
Deployments manage pods and ensure your desired replica count is maintained
Self-healing means Kubernetes automatically replaces failed pods
Scaling lets you change replica count with a single command
ReplicaSets are the object between Deployments and Pods
Rolling updates deploy new versions without downtime
Labels and selectors are how Kubernetes organizes and finds objects

lesson_emails.subject: Day 3: Kubernetes Networking
topics_covered: How Services find Pods using label selectors
key_concepts: Pod IPs change on every restart
Services provide stable endpoints - one address that routes to multiple pods
Label selectors connect Services to pods based on key-value labels
ClusterIP is internal only, default type, needs port-forward for external access
NodePort opens a port on the node for quick external access
DNS works inside the cluster - pods reach services by name
Port-forward creates a tunnel from your laptop to the cluster
what_you_learned_today: Pod IPs are ephemeral. They change on every restart.
Services provide stable endpoints. One address that routes to multiple pods.
Label selectors connect Services to pods based on key-value labels.
ClusterIP is internal only. Default type, needs port-forward for external access.
NodePort opens a port on the node for quick external access.
DNS works inside the cluster. Pods reach services by name.
Port-forward creates a tunnel from your laptop to the cluster.

lesson_emails.subject: Day 4: The real way to do Kubernetes
lesson_emails.file_name: Day 4_ The real way to do Kubernetes.eml
topics_covered: Anatomy of Kubernetes YAML: apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec
Multiple resources in one file with --- separator
key_concepts: YAML manifests define resources declaratively
apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec form the structure of every Kubernetes resource
kubectl apply creates or updates resources to match the file
Multiple resources can live in one file separated by ---
--dry-run=client -o yaml generates YAML from commands
Infrastructure as Code means your cluster state is version controlled
kubectl_commands: kubectl create deployment test --image=nginx --replicas=2 --dry-run=client -o yaml > test.yaml
kubectl create service clusterip test --tcp=80:80 --dry-run=client -o yaml
what_you_learned_today: YAML manifests define resources declaratively.
apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec form the structure of every Kubernetes resource.
kubectl apply creates or updates resources to match the file.
Multiple resources can live in one file separated by ---.
--dry-run=client -o yaml generates YAML from commands.
Infrastructure as Code means your cluster state is version controlled.

lesson_emails.subject: Day 5: Deploy something you'll actually use
lesson_emails.file_name: Day 5_ Deploy something you'll actually use.eml
key_concepts: Namespaces organize resources in your cluster
kubectl config set-context changes your default namespace
Environment variables configure containers
Multiple resources can live in one YAML file with --- separator
Containers are ephemeral - data doesn't persist by default
what_you_learned_today: Namespaces organize resources in your cluster.
kubectl config set-context changes your default namespace.
Environment variables configure containers.
Multiple resources can live in one YAML file with --- separator.
kubectl logs shows container output.
kubectl describe shows detailed resource information.
Containers are ephemeral. Data doesn't persist by default.

lesson_emails.subject: Day 6: Making your data survive in Kubernetes
lesson_emails.file_name: Day 6_ Making your data survive in Kubernetes.eml
topics_covered: Volume types: emptyDir, hostPath, PersistentVolumeClaim, configMap, secret
volumeMounts and volumes in pod spec
key_concepts: Containers are ephemeral - data doesn't persist by default
PersistentVolume (PV) is actual storage provisioned in the cluster
PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a request for storage
StorageClass defines how storage is provisioned
volumeMounts defines where to mount storage inside the container
volumes connects pods to PVCs
Data survives restarts because it lives outside the container
